# Mahāgopālaka Sutta (MN 33 (PTS MN i 220))

**ID:** MN 33 (PTS MN i 220)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)

**Title (Pali):** Mahāgopālaka Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 220

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāgopālaka Sutta* (MN 33) is set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park, where the Buddha addresses the monks with an extended pastoral simile [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The discourse enumerates eleven failings that prevent a cowherd from properly tending his herd, comparing them to eleven detrimental qualities that hinder a mendicant's spiritual growth; conversely, eleven positive qualities are taught that foster growth and maturity in the Dhamma [Hazra 1994; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Among the required skills of a monk is knowing the proper pasture, an image that signifies the contemplation of *satipaṭṭhāna* [Analayo 2006; Analayo 2010]. Another crucial factor is approaching experienced elder monks who preserve the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the *mātṛkā*s (*mātikā*) to question them and resolve interpretive perplexities [Analayo, Dawn of Abhidharma; Nance, Sūtra comm lit diss]. Drawing attention to the emphasis placed on venerating senior elders (*theras*), G. C. Pande considers this textual feature an indicator of the sutta's relatively late institutional composition [Pande 1974]. Dan Lusthaus further notes thematic affinities between this discourse and the *Pratītyasamutpādavibhaṅganirdeśasūtra* [Lusthaus 2002].

MN 33 shares an almost identical Pali parallel in the Aṅguttaranikāya (AN 11.17) [Donner 1976; Lamotte, Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra]. Beyond the Pali canon, parallels to the cowherd rules are attested in Chinese Āgamas, notably in Kumārajīva's translation *Fangniu jing* (T 123), the *Ekottarāgama* (EĀ 49.1 / T 125), and the *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 1249 / T 99), as well as Sanskrit fragments, the Tibetan *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* (D 6 / D 211), and Mahāyāna treatises such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra* (T 1509) and Śāntideva's *Śikṣāsamuccaya* [Donner 1976; Lamotte, Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra]. Anālayo points out that where MN 33 refers to learned monks who preserve the *mātṛkā*s, its *Saṃyuktāgama* parallel mentions the *Abhidharma*, reflecting early terminological developments between the early discourse and Vinaya traditions [Analayo, Dawn of Abhidharma].
